From Old Norse kjǫlr, from Proto-Germanic *keluz.

parole.significato: kind, species (a type, race or category)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kyn (“kin”), from Proto-Germanic *kunją (“kin, family, clan”), from Pre-Germanic *ǵn̥h₁-yo-m, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to produce, to beget, to give birth”). parole.significato: to smear (distribute in a thin layer))
parole.testo: From Old Norse klína, from Proto-Germanic *kleinijan-, from Proto-Indo-European *gley-. Compare Old High German klenan.

From Old Norse kné, from Proto-Germanic *knewą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu (“knee”).

parole.significato: knife (utensil or tool designed for cutting)
parole.testo: From Old Norse knífr, from Proto-Germanic *knībaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gneybʰ-.

parole.significato: form removed by a 2021 spelling decision; superseded by køl
parole.testo: From Old Norse kol, from Proto-Germanic *kulą (“coal”).

parole.significato: to come; to approach or move towards the speaker, another person, or another point of reference
parole.testo: The verb is inherited from Old Norse koma (“to come”), from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną (“to come”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (“to come, go”). The noun is a substantivization of the verb. Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk koma and komme, Danish komme, Swedish komma, Icelandic koma, Faroese koma, Eng
From Old Norse konungr and kongr, from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz (“king”).
From Old Norse konungdómr, from Proto-Germanic *kuningadōmaz. Equivalent to konge + -dømme.

From Old Norse konungríki, from Proto-Germanic *kuningarīkiją. Equivalent to konge (“king”) + rike (“realm”). Compare Danish kongerige, Swedish kungarike, Icelandic konungsríki, Dutch koninkrijk, German Königreich, Old English cyningrīċe, and Scots kinrick.
From Old Norse korn, from Proto-Germanic *kurną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm.
From Old Norse krabbi, from Proto-Germanic *krabbô, from Proto-Indo-European *grobʰ-.
From Old Norse krókr, from Proto-Germanic *krōkaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gerg-.

parole.significato: to ornament, decorate or embellish with painted, carved, embroidered or drawn figures, patterns or flourishes
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Norwegian krota (“to ornament, engrave”), from Old Norse krota (“to engrave, ornament”), probably from Proto-Germanic *krutōną (“to carve”). parole.significato: a rounded protrusion, lump, swelling or bump, especially on the body
parole.testo: Related to kule (“ball; lump, swelling”), from Old Norse kúla (“swelling, bump”), from Proto-Germanic *kūlǭ (“bump, swelling”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk kul, Swedish kul and kula, Icelandic kúla, German Kaule and Dutch kuil (“bump, swelling; pit, hollow”).

parole.significato: a circle, company, or group of people or other living beings
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse kúla (“swelling, bump”), from Proto-Germanic *kūlǭ (“lump, swelling”). The figurative senses developed through the ideas of a rounded mass, a gathered group, and a bounded occurrence or spell. From Old Norse kol, from Proto-Germanic *kulą, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷol-, from *ǵwelH- (“to burn, shine”).
From Old Norse kunna, from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃-.
From Old Norse kveld, from Proto-Germanic *kweldą, *kwildiz.
From Old Norse kvern, from Proto-Germanic *kwernō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷréh₂wō (“heavy stone”), from *gʷréh₂us (“heavy”)
From Old Norse koss, from Proto-Germanic *kussaz. Cognate to English kiss, German Kuss, Dutch kus.
From Old Norse kyssa, from Proto-Germanic *kussijaną.
Related to the noun kår, itself from the Old Norse kør and from Proto-Germanic *kuzą.

parole.significato: lively, frisky, high-spirited, merry; exuberant or playful
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse kátr (“happy, cheerful”), from Proto-Germanic *kanhtaz (“happy, glad”), of uncertain further origin. Kroonen tentatively connects the Proto-Germanic form with *genk- (“to gladden, rejoice”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk kåt, Icelandic kátur, Faroese kátur, Swedish kåt and Danis

parole.significato: to arouse, excite sexually; chiefly in kåte opp
parole.testo: From kåt (“frisky, lively; sexually aroused”) + -e (“infinitive suffix”). The adjective is from Old Norse kátr (“happy, cheerful”), from Proto-Germanic *kanhtaz (“happy, glad”).

parole.significato: a horny or sexually aroused person or animal
parole.testo: From kåt (“horny”) + -ing (“noun-forming suffix”), denoting a person or animal characterized by the adjective. The base adjective is from Old Norse kátr (“happy, cheerful”), from Proto-Germanic *kanhtaz (“happy, glad”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk kåting (“horny person or animal”).
From Old Norse hlaða, from Proto-Germanic *hlaþaną.

parole.significato: a layer (a single thickness of some material covering a surface)
parole.testo: From Old Norse lag (“layer; companionship”), from Proto-Germanic *lagą (“situation; law”), from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie”).

parole.significato: a district (area which is under common law and has common principal Things)
parole.testo: From Old Norse lǫg (“fate, situation; law”), from lag (“layer; companionship”), from Proto-Germanic *lagą (“situation; law”), from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie”).
From Old Norse lax (“salmon”), from Proto-Germanic *lahsaz, from Proto-Indo-European *laks- (“salmon”).

parole.significato: paralysed, paralyzed; lacking movement, strength, or sensation in all or part of the body
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse lami (“lame, crippled”), from Proto-Germanic *lamaz (“lame, weak, defective”). The modern strong form was probably reinforced by Danish lam (“lame, paralysed”), from Old Danish lam. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk lam, Swedish lam, Danish lam, Icelandic lami, Faroese lamin, Englis

parole.significato: a lamb; a young sheep, especially one less than a year old
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse lamb (“lamb”), from Proto-Germanic *lambaz (“lamb”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁l̥h₁-on-bʰ-os- (“lamb”), an enlargement of *h₁elh₁én (“deer, elk”), ultimately from *h₁el- (“deer, elk”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk lam, Danish lam, Swedish lamm, Icelandic lamb, Faroese lamb, E

parole.significato: (Solør) a hinge with a long, flat metal strap or plate fastened across part of a door
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse lǫm (“hinge, joint”), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *lamō (“hinge”). The further origin is uncertain. Compare Icelandic löm (“hinge”). Traditionally compared with Latin lamina (“thin plate, sheet of metal”).
From Old Norse land, from Proto-Germanic *landą, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”).
From Old Norse hlæja (“to laugh”), from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *klek-, *kleg- (“to shout”).
From Old Norse liðugr, from Proto-Germanic *liþugaz.

parole.significato: lefse; a soft, unleavened Norwegian flatbread, often spread with butter and sugar or served with savoury food
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse *leifsa (“flatbread”), probably an s-derivative of hleifr (“loaf, bread”), from Proto-Germanic *hlaibaz (“loaf, bread”); compare leiv (“rolled-out piece of flatbread or lefse; thick slice of bread”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk lefse, Swedish dialectal läfsa and Shetlandic lef
From Old Norse leggja, from Proto-Germanic *lagjaną. Cognates include Danish lægge, Swedish lägga, German legen, Dutch leggen, and English lay. Compare with ligge.

parole.significato: to hold hands with, to go hand in hand with (e.g. a child, a lover)
parole.testo: From dialectal Norwegian, from Old Norse leiða, from Proto-Germanic *laidijaną. Doublet of lede (“to lead”).

parole.significato: to play, to act in a manner such that one has fun
parole.testo: From Old Norse leika, from Proto-Germanic *laikaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyg-.

parole.significato: a last (a tool in the shape of a human foot, for shaping or preserving the shape of shoes)
parole.testo: From Old Norse leistr, from Proto-Germanic *laistaz.
From Old Norse léttr, from Proto-Germanic *linhtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-.

From Old Norse lifa, from Proto-Germanic *libjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leip- (“leave, cling, linger”). Cognate with Swedish leva, Danish leve, Icelandic lifa, Dutch leven, German leben, English live.
From Old Norse lifr, from Proto-Germanic *librō, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to smudge, stick”), from *ley- (“to be slimy, be sticky, glide”).

parole.significato: to lie (be in a horizontal position)
parole.testo: From Old Norse liggja, from Proto-Germanic *ligjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie down”). Cognates include Danish ligge, Swedish ligga, Gothic 𐌻𐌹𐌲𐌰𐌽 (ligan), German liegen, Dutch liggen, and English lie.
From Old Norse líkr, alternative spelling of glíkr, from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz.
Inherited from Old Norse lík, from Proto-Germanic *līką, from Proto-Indo-European *leyg-.
From Old Norse líka, from Proto-Germanic *līkāną.
From Old Norse lind, from Proto-Germanic *lindō.

From Old Norse líf (“life”), from Proto-Germanic *lībą (“body, life”), likely derived from *lībaną (“to remain, be left”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick; fat or stick substance”), from *ley-, *(s)ley- (“to slip, slide, glide; slimy”).

parole.significato: the act of lurking or wandering around aimlessly
parole.testo: loke + -ing, verbal noun form of loke (“to lurk; wander around aimlessly”), from Old Norse loka (“to let fall and hang down”). Last part from Old Norse -ingr m, -ingi m, -ing f, from Proto-Germanic *-ingō, *-ungō.

parole.significato: a louse (plural lice), or a similar animal, e.g. a sea louse
parole.testo: From Old Norse lús, from Proto-Germanic *lūs, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *luHs-, *lewH-.

parole.significato: describing plants mostly from the heather family, Ericaceae
parole.testo: From Old Norse lyng n, from Proto-Germanic *lingwą.

parole.significato: a fluid used in the boiling of plant material
parole.testo: From Old Norse lǫgr (“lake, liquid”), from Proto-Germanic *laguz, from Proto-Indo-European *lókus. Cognates include Latin lacus and Scottish Gaelic loch.
From Old Norse láss, from Proto-Germanic *lamsaz. The neuter gender was used in Riksmål at least since the early 20th century, probably as a borrowing from dialectal Norwegian.

parole.significato: to make, emit a sound; to sound
parole.testo: From Old Norse láta, from Proto-Germanic *lētaną. Doublet of la and late.
From Old Norse hlátr, derived from hlæja (“to laugh”), from Proto-Germanic *hlahtraz (whence Old English hleahtor and English laughter). Compare latter.

parole.significato: a leather armour for the upper body, sometimes combined with flexible metal armour
parole.testo: From lær + brynje, first part fom Old Norse leðr (“leather”), from Proto-Germanic *leþrą (“leather”), from Proto-Celtic *ɸlitro-, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥tro-. Last part from Old Norse brynja (“coat of mail or plate”), from Proto-Germanic *brunjǭ (“breastplate”), possibly from Old Irish bruinne

From Old Norse magr (“thin, meager”), from Proto-Germanic *magraz, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós.
From Old Norse malmr, from Proto-Germanic *malmaz. Doublet of malm.
From Old Norse mǫn, from Proto-Germanic *manō.

From Old Norse mergr, from Proto-Germanic *mazgaz < *mazgą, from Proto-Indo-European *mozgos, *mosgʰos. Compare Icelandic mergur, Swedish märg, Danish marv, Dutch merg, German Mark, English marrow.
From Old Norse með (“with, along with”), from Proto-Germanic *midi (“with, by, through; along, together”), from Proto-Indo-European *meth₂, from *me (“in the middle of, near, by, around, with”).
From Old Norse merr, from Proto-Germanic *marhijō (“female horse”).

parole.significato: most; used in construction of superlative of long/foreign adjectives
parole.testo: From Old Norse mestr, from Proto-Germanic *maist.

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse miðdagr (“midday, noon”), from Proto-Germanic *midjadagaz (“noon”), from *midjaz (“middle”) + *dagaz (“day”), literally “middle day” or “middle of the day”. From Old Norse mjǫðr, from Proto-Germanic *meduz (“mead”), from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu (“honey, mead”).
From moder, from Old Norse móðir, from Proto-Germanic *mōdēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.

parole.significato: a joint smoked in the morning
parole.testo: morgning + -ings, first part from the verb morgne (“to dawn, wake up”), from Old Norse morgna (“to dawn (become morning)”). Last part is a variant of -ing, from Old Norse -ingr m, -ingi m, -ing f, from Proto-Germanic *-ingō, *-ungō.

parole.significato: a traditional Norwegian sausage made from chopped or ground offal, often mixed with other meat
parole.testo: From morr (“chopped or ground offal; sausage made from such offal”) + pølse (“sausage”), literally “offal sausage”. The first element is from Old Norse mǫrr (“fat, tallow”), from Proto-Germanic *marhwaz (“tallow, suet”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *merk- (“to decay”). Compare Norwe
From Old Norse múli, from Proto-Germanic *mūlô.

parole.significato: any plant of the potentilla family
parole.testo: From Old Norse mura, from Proto-Germanic *murhǭ.

parole.significato: Existing in large quantities: lots of, a lot (of), many, a great deal (of), much (antonym to lite, "small", "little")
parole.testo: From eastern Norwegian dialects, from Old Norse mykit, younger variant of mikit, neuter form of mikill (“big”), from Proto-Germanic *mikilaz, which see. Introduced in 1917 as a byform of meget, from Danish meget, and made the sole standard form in 1938 (though meget survives as an adverb).

parole.significato: a mosquito (small flying insect of the family Culicidae, known for biting and sucking blood)
parole.testo: From Old Norse mý, from Proto-Germanic *mugjō, *mują, *muwō (“midge”), from Proto-Indo-European *mū- (“fly, midge”), *mu-, *mew-. Compare Swedish mygga, Danish myg, Icelandic mý, English midge, West Frisian mich, Dutch mug, Low German mügge, German Mücke.

parole.significato: a given dimension; measurement (a measure of spatial extent in a particular direction, such as height, width or breadth…
parole.testo: From Old Norse mál (“measurement, size”), from Proto-Germanic *mēlą (“measure, time; occasion”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁lom, from *meh₁- (“to measure”).

parole.significato: a voice (sound uttered by the mouth, especially by human beings in speech or song)
parole.testo: From Old Norse mál (“language, speech”), from Proto-Germanic *maþlą (“gathering; speech”), of *mōtaną (“to be allowed, to be permitted to, may”), from Proto-Indo-European *mōd- (“to permit, make able”), of *med- (“to measure, give advice, heal”).

parole.significato: a moon; a natural satellite orbiting a planet or another larger celestial body
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse máni (“moon”), from Proto-Germanic *mēnô (“moon”), from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”), from earlier *méh₁n̥s-s, probably from *meh₁- (“to measure”). Doublet of måned (“month”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk måne, Danish måne, Swedish måne, Icelandic máni, Faroese

parole.significato: a ridge (highest point on a roof)
parole.testo: From Old Norse mœnir, from Proto-Germanic *mōnijaz.
From Old Norse meyrr, from Proto-Germanic *marwaz.
Possibly related to Old Norse merja (“to strike, crush”), from Proto-Germanic *marzijaną. In sense 2, probably influenced by ildmørje (“fire-mass, glowing embers”). Compare mølje.
From Old Norse myrkr, from Proto-Germanic *mirkwijaz. Cognate to English murk.
From Old Norse nátt, from Proto-Germanic *nahts (“night”), from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts (“night”).
From Old Norse nǫf f, from Proto-Germanic *nabō.

parole.significato: a rough hand drill, an auger (traditionally used to bore large holes in wheel hubs)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse nafarr (“auger”), from Proto-Germanic *nabagaizaz (“auger”), from *nabō (“nave, hub”) + *gaizaz (“spear”). By surface analysis, nav + geir) Compare Norwegian Nynorsk navar, Swedish navare, Danish naver, Icelandic nafarr and English auger.

parole.significato: down (from a higher to a lower level)
parole.testo: From Old Norse niðr, from Proto-Germanic *niþer.
From Old Norse nei, from Proto-Germanic *nai (“never”), *nē (“not”), from Proto-Indo-European *né, *nē, *nēy (negative particle).

From Old Norse níu (whence also Danish ni, Icelandic níu, Faroese níggju and Swedish nio) from Proto-Germanic *newun, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognate with Gothic 𐌽𐌹𐌿𐌽 (niun); Old English niġon (English nine); Old Frisian nigun (West Frisian njoggen); Old High German niun (German neun).
From Old Norse nítján, from Proto-Germanic *newuntehun.

parole.significato: a foreigner who is fond of Norway and Norwegians (literally; friend of Norway)
parole.testo: Norge + -s- + venn, first part from Old Norse Norðvegr, from both norðr (“north”), from Proto-Germanic *nurþrą (“north, northern”), from *nurþraz (“north, northern”), from Pre-Germanic *h₁nŕ̥t(e)ros, from Proto-Indo-European *nér (“under (the surface)”) + vegr (“way, road”), from Proto-Germanic *weg

parole.significato: Norse (of or relating to ancient or mediaeval Norway or Scandinavia)
parole.testo: From Old Norse norrœnn, norrǿnn and norðrœnn, norðrǿnn, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrōnijaz.
From Old Norse nǫs, from Proto-Germanic *nasō, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s.
From Old Norse nýr, from Proto-Germanic *niwjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos (“new”).
From Old Norse hnjósa (“to sneeze”), from Proto-Germanic *hneusaną.
From Old Norse nár (“corpse; a dead person”), from Proto-Germanic *nawiz (“corpse”), from Proto-Indo-European *neh₂wis (“corpse”), from *neh₂w- (“death; corpse”).
From Old Norse nál, from Proto-Germanic *nēþlō.
From Old Norse ok (“and”), from earlier auk (“and”), from Proto-Germanic *auk (“also, too, furthermore”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewg- (“to increase, enlarge”).
From Old Norse oxi, uxi, from Proto-Germanic *uhsô, from Proto-Indo-European *uksḗn (“ox, bull”).

parole.significato: alder (a tree of the Alnus genus)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ǫlr (compare Icelandic elri, Danish el, Swedish al), from Proto-Germanic *aluz, *alusō (compare English alder), variant of *alizō, *alisō (compare Dutch els, German Erle), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisos.

From Old Norse um, from Proto-Germanic *umbi (“around, about”). See cognates Dutch om and German um. As a conjunction, um superseded or blended with Old Norse ef and em, taking on their function as well. This is from Proto-Germanic *jabai (“when, if”), whence also English if and German ob.

parole.significato: round (of drinks, contest, boxing match etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Norse umgangr, from Proto-Germanic *umbigangaz; also from omgå and omgås.

parole.significato: a word (a distinct unit of language with a particular meaning)
parole.testo: From Old Norse orð, from Proto-Germanic *wurdą, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo- (“word”). Cognates include Danish ord, Swedish ord, German Wort, and English word.
From Old Norse ormr (“snake, worm”), from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz (“worm, snake”), from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis (“worm”), possibly from *wer- (“to burn”).

orm + -e- + yngel, first part from Old Norse ormr (“snake, worm”), from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz (“worm, snake”), from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis (“worm”), possibly from *wer- (“to burn”). Last part from the verb yngle (“create, procreate, grow”), from the adjective ung (“young”), from Old Norse ungr

From Old Norse ofn, from Proto-Germanic *uhnaz, *uhwnaz (compare Danish ovn, Swedish ugn, Icelandic ofn, Dutch oven, Low German Aven, West Frisian ûne, German Ofen, Gothic auhns), probably from a Proto-Indo-European *aukw- (“cooking pot”), *Hukʷ-, *ukwnos.
From Old Norse padda, from Proto-Germanic *paddǭ.

parole.significato: to peck or strike with the beak
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse pikka (“to hack, prick”), originally imitative of a short tapping or striking sound and traditionally connected with Proto-Germanic *pikkōną (“to pick, peck, prick, knock”). parole.testo: From Old Norse þorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą, whence also German Dorf, German Low German Dörp, Dorp, Daarp and Dutch dorp.
From Old Norse torf, from Proto-Germanic *turbz (“turf, lawn”), from Proto-Indo-European *dorbh- (“tuft, grass”).

From Old Norse tré (“tree; beam”), from Proto-Germanic *trewą (“tree”), from pre-Germanic *dréwom, from Proto-Indo-European *dóru (“tree”), possibly from *drew- (“hard, firm, strong, solid”). The plurals trær and trærne are derived from Danish træ.
From Old Norse tregr (“unwilling, slow”), from Proto-Germanic *tregaz (“sad, unwilling”).
From Old Norse trǫll, from Proto-Germanic *truzlą, from Proto-Indo-European *dreh₂-.

parole.significato: thrush, one of several species of songbirds of the family Turdidae
parole.testo: From Old Norse þrǫstr, from Proto-Germanic *þrasduz, from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos. Compare Swedish trast, Icelandic þröstur, Faroese trøstur.
From Old Norse tryggr, from Proto-Germanic *triwwiz.
From Old Norse *þrykkia, from Proto-Germanic *þrukkijaną.

parole.significato: to practise magic or sorcery; to cast spells
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse trylla (“to enchant; turn into a troll”), from Proto-Germanic *truzlijaną (“to perform magic, conjure”), a causative or denominative derivative of *truzlą (“troll, supernatural being”). The original sense was “to turn someone into a troll”, hence more generally “to transform

parole.significato: to tread, step, set foot (på / on)
parole.testo: Partially from a dialectal Norwegian descendant of Old Norse troða, from Proto-Germanic *trudaną. Partially backformed from the past forms trådte, trådt of Danish træde (Bokmål tre), from Middle Low German trēden, ultimately from the same root.
From Old Norse þráðr, from Proto-Germanic *þrēduz, from Proto-Indo-European *treh₁-tu-, from *terh₁- (“rub, twist”).
From Old Norse þungr, from Proto-Germanic *þunguz.
From Old Norse þúsund, from Proto-Germanic *þūsundī.

parole.significato: a twin (either of two people who shared the same uterus at the same time, or of two similar or closely related objects)
parole.testo: Related to Old Norse tvinnr, tvennr and Nynorsk tvinn and tvenn. Possibly from an Old Norse root *tvinlingr, from Proto-Germanic *twinilingaz, with the first element from *twinaz. Compare Danish and Swedish tvilling, English twinling, Dutch tweeling, German Zwilling.
From Old Norse tyggja, tyggva, from Proto-Germanic *kewwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁-.
From Old Norse þyngd, from Proto-Germanic *þungiþō.

parole.significato: German (relating to Germany and the German people)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þýðverskr, þýzkr, from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz (“of or relating to a people”), from Proto-Germanic *þeudō (“people, nation”), from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂ (“people”).

parole.significato: Forms words with a negative, lacking, or opposite meaning.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse ú- (“un-, not”), also ó- (“un-, not”), from Proto-Germanic *un- (“un-, not”), from Proto-Indo-European *n̥- (“not”), zero-grade of *ne (“not”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk u-, Danish u-, Swedish o-, Icelandic ó-, Faroese ó-, English un-, German un-, Dutch on-, Latin in-, and A

From u- + forsonlig, first part from Old Norse ú-, ó-, from Proto-Germanic *un-, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-, a prefix use of the particle *né (“not”). Last part from the verb forsone (“reconcile”), from Middle Low German vorsōnen or German versöhnen (“reconcile”), from Middle High German versüene

From uforsonlig + -het, firt part u- from Old Norse ú-, ó-, from Proto-Germanic *un-, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-, a prefix use of the particle *né (“not”) + uforsonlig from the verb forsone (“reconcile”), from Middle Low German vorsōnen or German versöhnen (“reconcile”), from Middle High German v

From Old Norse úlíkr, from Proto-Germanic *ungalīkaz. By surface analysis, u- + lik (“similar”). Compare Old English unġelīċ (English unlike), Dutch ongelijk, Faroese ólíkur, German ungleich, Swedish olik.
From Old Norse ull, from Proto-Germanic *wullō.
From Old Norse undir, from Proto-Germanic *under.
From Old Norse undr, from Proto-Germanic *wundrą, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish for, desire, strive for, win, love”).

parole.significato: young (in the early part of life or growth)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ungr (“young”), from Proto-Germanic *jungaz (“young”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁n̥ḱós (“young”).
From Old Norse út, from Proto-Germanic *ūt.

parole.significato: exit, way out (to be used by pedestrians).
parole.testo: From Old Norse útgangr (út + gangr), from Proto-Germanic *ūtgangaz. Equivalent to ut + gang. Compare inngang, undergang, avgang, and oppgang.
From Old Norse úveðr, óveðr, from Proto-Germanic *unwedrą, equivalent to u- + vær; compare with German Unwetter, Norwegian Nynorsk uvêr, Swedish oväder and English unweather.
From Old Norse vaða, from Proto-Germanic *wadaną.

parole.significato: a valkyrie; female attendant of Odin that leads fallen warriors to Valhalla
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old Norse valkyrja, from Proto-Germanic *walakuzjǭ.
From Old Norse vargr, from Proto-Germanic *wargaz.

parole.significato: at, by, near, on (near or next to)
parole.testo: From Old Norse við and viðr (compare the prefix veder-), from Proto-Germanic *wiþrą (“against”). Cognates include Danish ved, Swedish vid, German wider (“against”), and English with.

parole.significato: wood, firewood (any wooden material that is gathered and used for fuel)
parole.testo: From Old Norse viðr, from Proto-Germanic *widuz. Cognate with Swedish ved, Old English wudu (English wood) and Old High German witu.
From Old Norse vel, from Proto-Germanic *wela, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-.
From Old Norse vinstri, from Proto-Germanic *winistraz.
From Old Norse verk, related to yrke (“profession”) and virke (“to function”). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *werką, from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵom.

From Old Norse vernd, vǫrn (“defence”), from Proto-Germanic *warīniz (“warding off, defense”), from *warjaną (“to ward off, defend against”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to watch, guard, heed, notice”) + Proto-Germanic *-īniz (forms abstract nouns).

parole.significato: to weave (form something by passing strands of material over and under one another)
parole.testo: From Old Norse vefa, from Proto-Germanic *webaną, from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to weave”). Compare with Danish væve, Swedish väva, Faroese veva, Icelandic vefa.
From Old Norse víðr.

parole.significato: dedicate something to someone or towards a cause
parole.testo: From Old Norse vígja, from Proto-Germanic *wīhijaną.
From Old Norse vík, from Proto-Germanic *wīkō.
From Old Norse villr, from Proto-Germanic *wilþijaz. Cognates include English wild.

From Old Norse vinna, from Proto-Germanic *winnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to strive, wish, desire, love”). Related to Swedish and Icelandic vinna, English win, Dutch winnen, Danish vinde and German gewinnen.

parole.significato: to know (be certain or sure about (something); have knowledge of)
parole.testo: From Old Norse vita, from Proto-Germanic *witaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“see”). Cognates include English wit and Latin video.
From Old Norse víf, from Proto-Germanic *wībą. Cognate with English wife.
From Old Norse verða, from Proto-Germanic *werþaną (“to become, happen”).

parole.significato: to wake or wake up, to awaken
parole.testo: From Old Norse vakna, from Proto-Germanic *waknaną.

parole.significato: a thin, flexible branch, twig, stick, rod, or stalk
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse vǫndr (“branch, twig, stick”), from Proto-Germanic *wanduz (“rod, switch, stick”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wendʰ- (“to turn, twist, weave, braid”). Related by ablaut to vinde (“to wind, twist”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk vånd, Icelandic vöndur, Danish vånd, Goth
From Old Norse vátr, from Proto-Germanic *wētaz.
From dialectal Norwegian, from Old Norse ver, from Proto-Germanic *warją (“embankment, dam”), which see.
From Old Norse væta (“wetness”), from Proto-Germanic *wētijǭ (“wetness”). Compare Danish væde, Icelandic væta, Swedish väta.
From Old Norse væta (“wet, make wet”), from Proto-Germanic *wētijaną (“wet”). Compare Danish væde, Icelandic væta, Swedish väta.

From the verb yngle (“create, procreate, grow”), from the adjective ung (“young”), from Old Norse ungr (“young”), from Old Norse ungr (“young”), from Proto-Germanic *jungaz (“young”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁n̥ḱós (“young”), from *h₂yuh₁en- (“young”), from both *h₂óyu (“long time, lifetime”)

Inherited from Old Norse á (“stream, river”), from Proto-Germanic *ahwō (“stream, river; water”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ékʷeh₂ (“water”). Cognate with Icelandic á, Faroese á, Swedish å, Danish å, Old English ēa and German Ache (“stream, river”).

parole.significato: to; an infinitive marker placed before a verb in the infinitive
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse at (“at, by, to; infinitive marker”), from Proto-Germanic *at (“at, toward”). The use as an infinitive marker developed from the directional meaning of the preposition, comparable to the use of English to, German zu and French à before infinitives. The word was officially wr

From Old Norse ok, from Proto-Germanic *juką, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm. Cognate with Latin iugum (English jugular), Sanskrit युग (yugá, “yoke, team”), Old Church Slavonic иго (igo) (whence Russian иго (igo)), Persian یوق (yowq). Compare English yoga. Doublet of yoga.

parole.significato: a field (wide, open space that is usually used to grow crops)
parole.testo: From Old Norse akr, ákr, from Proto-Germanic *akraz (“field”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵros (“field”). Akin to English acre.
From Old Norse *áma, from Proto-Germanic *ēmǭ (“larva”).

parole.significato: a short right ski that was used together with a longer left ski
parole.testo: From Old Norse ǫndurr m, from Proto-Germanic *anduraz.
From Old Norse ár (“year; plenty, abundance”), from Proto-Germanic *jērą (“year”), from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year”).

parole.significato: love (a profound and caring affection towards someone)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ást (“love”), from Proto-Germanic *anstiz (“favour, affection”), from both *unnaną (“to grant, bestow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃n̥-né-h₂-ti, from the root *h₃neh₂- (“to enjoy”) + and from *stiz.

Inherited from Old Norse ek (“I”), from Proto-Germanic *ek (“I”), from Proto-Indo-European *éǵh₂óm (“I”). The form represents dialectal developments in which the final consonant disappeared and the vowel developed into /æː/. The related form æg (“I”) retains the final consonant. Compare Norwegian Ny
From Old Norse auka, from Proto-Germanic *aukaną. Cognate with Latin augēo (“to increase”).
From Old Norse øx (“axe”), from Proto-Germanic *akwisī, from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷs-ih₂- (“axe”), from *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”).
From Old Norse ósk, from Proto-Germanic *wunskaz, *wunskō (“wish, desire”), from Proto-Indo-European *wun-, *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”).

parole.significato: to wish, to desire (softer and more polite version of want)
parole.testo: From Old Norse œskja, from Proto-Germanic *wunskijaną (“to wish”).
From Old Norse ǫrn, from Proto-Germanic *arô.

From Old Norse ey (“island”), from Proto-Germanic *awjō (“floodplain, meadow, island”), from earlier *agwjō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ékʷeh₂ (“water”). Cognate with English ey, eyot, oe, ait, and German Aue.
